NAT here rations inbound rather than blocking it, and the vendor states it in one line: 'Private /24 subnet per customer with 2 dedicated TCP ports per VPS', expanded on the homepage as 'NAT architecture with full IPv4 connectivity' and on the ports page as 'Your nat VPS is provided with 2 open TCP ports and 2 UDP port. By design the 1st TCP port is mapped to your VPS port 22/TCP.' Those forwards are the whole of the IPv4 inbound surface, the first TCP port is spent on SSH, so one TCP port and two UDP ports remain for a service, and they do not land on an address the VPS owns: the same page prints 'external_ip=x.y.z.w #The Hypervisor public IP'. The private network is a 10.0.0.0/8 subnet per customer and reaches the internet only through those forwards; what the vendor describes as 'full port-range access between locations with each other' is inter-VPS traffic and not a route in from outside. Two documented escapes exist. What stops a sustained workload is speed shaping rather than a byte allowance, 'We do not give any specific arbitrary GB or TB number, it is simply not practical with the TierHive model. Instead, we do performance tiers mixed with a FUP/QoS system.' applied as 'if you use 100 Mbit/s for 1 hour on average, we will globally limit your speed to 90 Mbit/s. If you then use 90 Mbit/s for the following hour on average, we will limit you to 80 Mbit/s, and we repeat this until you are down to 10 Mbit/s. For each hour you are 10 Mbit/s under the current cap, we add 10 Mbit/s back, until you are back to 100 Mbit/s.' over per-location caps of 50 to 225 Mbit/s. Two numbers fix what that means in practice. Singapore and Sydney at 75 Mbit/s leave 62% utilisation and Tokyo at 50 Mbit/s leaves 93%, with nothing spare. The port budget is the first wall for anything that wants several services on one address, the ratchet is the wall for anything that wants the whole cap, and 10 TiB of hot storage does not meet this product at any configuration, since the HDD slider stops at 4000 GB, which is 3.6 TiB.
